          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
IA No. 1566/2023
1. This prayer made in this application already stands rejected
vide order dated 18.03.2025 passed by this Court. Therein, the
applicant-Corporation  was  granted  liberty  to  move  this  Court
through an appropriate application after undertaking necessary
changes in the proposal.
2. In that view of the matter, the instant IA is formally
dismissed with the aforestated liberty.
I.A. Nos.1572 & 1573/2023
3. These applications have been filed by the Uttar Pradesh State
Bridge Corporation (in short, ‘UPSBC’) seeking felling of 76 and
249 trees, respectively, for the purpose of:
(i) Four lane Rail Overpass Bridge on Railway Crossing Number
10 A of Railway Kilometre 10/3-4 on Idgah–Bandikui Rail
Section from Bodla to Bichpuri route in Agra District, Uttar
Pradesh; and
(ii) For construction of bridge on the Yamuna River at Renuka
Dham to access the Runkata Baldev Marg in Agra District, Uttar
Pradesh.
4. The CEC granted permission to fell 98 trees and translocate 17
trees with respect to the prayer in I.A. No.1572/2023 and to fell
3

--- Page 48 ---
198 trees in I.A. No.1573 of 2023, i.e., interference was allowed
in respect of 313 trees, subject to the following conditions:
“a. Except for trees permitted to be felled or translocated no
other  tree  shall  be  felled/translocated/damaged  for
implementation of the project and in case any extra tree is
felled/damaged a penalty of Rs.100,000/- (Rs. One lakh only)
shall be charged from the applicant by the Divisional Forest
Officer, Agra;
b. In the two proposals (Application Nos. 1572 & 1573 of
2023) being recommended a total of 313 trees are being
affected. Hence the Divisional Forest Officer, Agra shall
undertake compensatory planting of 3130 saplings in lieu of
these 313 affected trees. These 3130 saplings shall be of
indigenous species of minimum 6 to 8 ft height in the allotted
9.699 ha. of barren land bearing Gata No. 38 in Village
Bichola, Tehsil Fatehabad, District Agra, Uttar Pradesh at the
cost of the Applicant, U.P. State Bridge Corporation Limited.
The area left after the compensatory afforestation of these
3130 trees will be planted and maintained by the Uttar Pradesh
Forest Department from its own budget;
c. to protect this plantation there shall be provision of a 4
ft high chain-link fence on a 2 feet high concrete/brick
footwall to protect the trees from being browsed by cattle and
other animals. Such boundary of this allotted 9.699 ha. of
barren land bearing Gata No.38 in Village Bichola, Fathabad,
District Agra, Uttar shall be erected by the forest department
at the cost of the Applicant;
d. there  shall  be  a  provision  for  the  protection  and
maintenance of these 3130 plants for the next ten years with
the cost to be borne by the applicant;
e. permission for the felling of trees under the Uttar
Pradesh Protection of Trees Act, 1976 may be granted by the
Forest Department only after the funds required for raising
the compensatory planting including the cost of fencing and
maintenance of the planted trees for ten years are deposited
with the Forest Department;
f. the allotted 9.699 ha. of barren land bearing Gata No. 38
in Village Bichola, Fathabad, District Agra, Uttar Pradesh

1. IA No.186517/2026 seeking impleadment of complainant

4. This appeal arises from an order of the High Court 1
dated 24.03.2026 whereby the anticipatory bail prayer
of the appellant in connection with FIR No.322/2025 at
P.S.  Crime  Branch,  Delhi  under  Sections
318(4)/336(3)/338/340(2)/61(2)/3(5)  of  the  Bhartiya

11 High Court of Delhi at New Delhi
1

--- Page 61 ---
M/s MG Leasing & Finance; (ii) Mr. Mohit Gogia; (iii)

allegations, inter alia, are in respect of cheating
the complainant of his money by assuring transfer of
properties  purchased  in  an  auction  under  the

and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2000 (for
short,  SARFAESI  act)  at  reasonable  rates.  The

8. The aforesaid interim order has been extended from
time to time though the Court was informed that on few
dates  the  appellant  could  not  cooperate  in  the
investigation as he was implicated in a case of money
laundering. According to the appellant during this
period,  he  had  applied  for  anticipatory  and  was
5

--- Page 65 ---
awaiting its outcome. Since the appellant had been
pursuing grant of anticipatory bail in the money
laundering matter, the matter was adjourned and the
interim protection was extended.  
9. However, the appellant’s prayer for anticipatory bail
in the money laundering matter came to be dismissed by
the  High  Court  and  thereafter  the  special  leave
petition preferred against the rejection order of the
High Court has also been dismissed.
10. The submission on behalf of the appellant is that
dismissal of the anticipatory bail prayer in the money
laundering matter would not come in the way of the
appellant  seeking  anticipatory  bail  in  these
proceedings as this case would have to be considered
on its own merits.  
11. In Dhanraj Aswani v. Amar S. Mulchandani and Another,
(2024) 10 SCC 336 , the issue before this Court was
whether a person in jail in connection with one case
could  seek  anticipatory  bail  in  another  case.
Answering the question in the affirmative, a three
Judge Bench of this Court held that no restriction can
be read into Section 438 of CrPC precluding accused
from applying for anticipatory bail in relation to an
offence, while in custody in different offence. It was
6

--- Page 66 ---
held that an accused is entitled to seek anticipatory
bail so long he is not arrested in connection with
that offence. 
12. In the light of the aforesaid decision, we are of the
view that rejection of appellant’s bail in money
laundering matter would not affect his right to seek
for anticipatory bail in the present matter where he
has not been arrested thus far.
13. Accordingly, we have proceeded to hear the learned
counsel  for  the  parties  to  consider  whether  the
appellant is entitled for anticipatory bail in the
present case.
14. Learned counsel for the appellant submitted that in
the present case a chargesheet has been submitted
against the accused who were named in the FIR.  The
chargesheet,  which  is  on  record,  indicates  that
investigation is pending against the appellant only
because there have been money transactions between the
main accused and the appellant.
15. It is contended on behalf of the appellant that the
money  transactions  between  the  appellant  and  the
accused were since much prior to the commission of
alleged offences which are subject matter of present
7

--- Page 67 ---
FIR. Besides those transactions are lawful of which
explanation  can  be  provided  by  the  appellant,
therefore, there is no requirement for a custodial
interrogation in the present case.  It is also the
case of the appellant that nothing incriminating had
been recovered from the possession of the appellant,
despite there being a raid on his house. In such
circumstances,  it  has  been  submitted  that  the
appellant is entitled for confirmation of the interim
protection granted earlier.
16. Per contra, on behalf of the respondents, it has been
submitted that the investigation thus far has revealed
that when the raid was conducted at the premises of
the appellant, the appellant had escaped with a bag
full  of  documents,  and  that  bag  was  ultimately
recovered from one Harsh.  Those documents reveal that
various e-stamps have been purchased in the name of
the appellant for dealing in property.  Besides there
is recovery of a photocopy of document relating to the
property which is subject matter of the present FIR.
In those circumstances, it has been submitted that
once it is proved that the appellant was transacting
with the accused, and documents recovered indicate the
involvement of the appellant, and investigation may
8

--- Page 68 ---
provide link to transactions relating to properties
which are non-existent, custodial interrogation is
warranted. 
17. In response to the above submission, the learned
counsel for the appellant submits that insofar as the
recovery  of  that  bag  from  Harsh  is  concerned,
documents  found  therein  are  not  ex  facie
incriminating. Moreover, if those were the documents
for which the investigating agency carried out raid,
they  have  already  achieved  what  they  wanted  to
achieve. It is further contended that purchase of E-
stamps by itself is not an offence as it would not
amount to creating a fabricated document. Besides,
there is no material to disclose that those documents
have any connection with the crime reported in the
subject FIR. In such circumstances, it has been prayed
that  the  interim  protection  granted  earlier  be
confirmed.  
18. We have considered the rival submissions and have gone
through the papers brought on record.  At this stage,
we are not supposed to deal with various documents
placed before us to record our opinion on the merits
of the case, as it would prejudice not only the
investigation, but also the trial which may ensue.  In
9

--- Page 69 ---
such circumstances, what we would have to consider is
whether in the subject FIR, custodial interrogation of
the appellant is required or not.  
19. In that context, what weighs with us is the fact that
the appellant had been in business transactions with
the accused since much before lodging of the subject
FIR.  Besides, the documents recovered from Harsh do
not prima facie disclose a connection with the crime
reported in the subject FIR.  Though, however, there
is one document, marked ‘D-9E’, which relates to
photocopy of certain documents connecting Jaskaran
Singh and Mohit Gogia in connection with auction of
Flat bearing No.220, 20 th Floor, Tower DLF Camallias,
DLG Golf Course, Sector 42, Gurgaon – 53.  However, it
is not clear as to what is its significance as also
whether it bears signature of either the appellant or
any of his close associates. In such circumstances, in
our  view,  if  the  appellant  co-operates  in
investigation the purpose would be served. Therefore,
in  our  view,  having  regard  to  the  nature  of
allegations in the FIR of the present case, the
interim protection granted earlier deserves to be
confirmed subject to the condition that the appellant
shall cooperate in the investigation and shall submit
10

--- Page 70 ---
himself for interrogation as and when required by the
investigating agency. Besides, the appellant would
have to submit his specimen writing/signatures for the
purposes of comparison of his writing from any of the
disputed documents, if the investigating agency so
requires.
20. In conclusion, we deem it appropriate to dispose of
this appeal by making the interim protection order
absolute subject to the following conditions:
(i) The  appellant  shall  appear  before  the
Investigating Officer of the subject FIR on
25.09.2026  at  the  office  of  Assistant
Commissioner of Police, Inter-State Cell,
Crime Branch, Chanakyapuri between 11.00
A.M. and 12.00 Noon;
(ii) Thereafter, the appellant shall cooperate
with  the  investigation  as  per  the
requirement of the Investigating Agency;
(iii) Within three weeks from today the appellant
shall  furnish  bail  bonds  to  the
satisfaction of the Trial Court concerned
along with an undertaking that he shall not
threaten  any  witness  or  tamper  the
11

--- Page 71 ---
evidence; and
(iv) The appellant shall not leave the country
without permission of the Trial Court.
21. In  addition  to  above,  the  earlier  order  dated
21.07.2026 requiring the appellant to surrender his
passport before the Registry of this Court shall
continue subject to the modification that the Registry
of this Court which has received the Passport shall
transmit the Passport to the Trial Court concerned. 
22. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  also  stand
disposed of.

MISCELLANEOUS APPLICATION NO.      OF 2026
[DIARY NO(S).49007/2026]
IN
WRIT PETITION(C) NO.581/2024
O R D E R
1. Initially, in para 6 of our order dated 08.12.2025
passed in WP (C) No. 581/2024, we directed that “ 30% of the
total seats in the State Bar Council shall be represented by
women members of the Bar Associations. Out of these, 20% be
filled up by way of election and 10% by way of co-option.”
2. In furtherance thereof, submissions were made by members
of the Bar with regard to the zone of consideration for the
purpose of co-option of the women members of the State Bar
Councils (SBCs). On a suggestion proffered by the Court,
there was broad consensus that the Chief Justices of the
jurisdictional High Courts may be authorised to nominate the
co-opted women members to the State Bar Councils.
3. Accordingly, the order dated 04.08.2026 was passed,
containing the following directions in para 3: 
2

--- Page 86 ---
“We,  accordingly,  direct  that  the  two  women
candidates to be co-opted to the State Bar Councils
shall be from the following categories: 
(i) former women Judges of the jurisdictional
High Court, or 
(ii) senior women members of the Bar having fair
standing and belonging to the concerned
State/States/UTs.”
4. The  instant  Miscellaneous  Applications  seek
modification  of  our  order  dated  04.08.2026.  The
Applicants seek a direction that either (i) the elected
members of the SBC, through a transparent, democratic
process, elect the two co-opted members; or (ii) the
positions earmarked for co-option be filled by the
unelected women candidates, who secured the highest
number  of  votes  in  the  respective  SBC  elections.
Certain  concerns  were  also  raised  regarding  the
eligibility of women advocates to be nominated for co-
option, the meaning of the term “senior”, as well as
the permissibility of nominating a former Judge of the
respective High Court. 
5. We have heard and considered all the submissions as well
as suggestions made by the counsel on both sides.
6. It is already clarified in para 4 of our order dated
04.08.2026 that the women advocates, who contested the SBC
elections  but  were  unsuccessful  in  the  same,  are  also
eligible for nomination under the method of co-option.
3

--- Page 87 ---
7. Further, the use of the word “senior” in para 3 of the
said order is not to be construed as only those persons who
are  designated  as  ‘senior  advocates’.  Rather,  it  means
someone who has been in practice for a substantially long
period of time and is found suitable by the elected members
of the SBC as well as shortlisted by the Chief Justice of
the respective High Court.
8. Additionally, we do not view the bar contained in
Article 220 of the Constitution against practice by former
Chief Justices and Judges of the High Courts as any kind of
impediment to their co-option into the respective SBC. By
virtue of becoming a member of the SBCs, they are not
required  to  resume  practice  before  the  respective  High
Courts.
9. Finally, it goes without saying that since the SBC of
Tripura  only  comprises  fifteen  members,  only  one  woman
member would be co-opted.
10. With these clarifications, we dispose of the instant
Miscellaneous Applications.
11. While doing so, we would like to reiterate that this
initiative  of  ensuring  adequate  representation  to  women
members of the Bar has occurred for the first time and is a
4

--- Page 88 ---
welcome  step  in  our  collective  journey  towards  equal
representation of women in the legal profession. While it is
difficult to ensure nomination for all, we believe this
court-created  mechanism,  guaranteeing  them  a  place  in
elected  offices,  will  encourage  women  lawyers  to  come
forward and contest Bar Council elections in even greater
numbers. We also believe that with the due course of time,
the Parliament as well as the Executive Authorities will
provide an appropriate mechanism for women representation in
the various Bar Councils. Until then, the instant mechanism
will continue to remain in force.

1
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL  NO.         OF 2026
(@ SLP(C) No.25843/2026)
RAJESH K. MEHTA                                    APPELLANT(s)
                                VERSUS
HDFC BANK LIMITED                                  RESPONDENT(S)
WITH
CIVIL APPEAL  NO.         OF 2026
(@SLP(C) No(s).28456/2026)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. Two sets of appeals are placed before us for consideration.
Civil Appeal @ SLP (C) 25843/2026 is filed by the appellant –
Rajesh K. Mehta, aggrieved over the condition imposed by the
High Court, while granting permission to travel abroad and
Civil Appeal @ SLP (C) 28456/2026 has been filed by the
appellant-Lilavati Kirtilal Mehta Medical Trust (for short,
‘the Trust’) after seeking leave, since the said appellant was
not a party before the High Court.
3. These appeals before us lie on a very narrow compass. 
4. By way of the impugned order dated 16.07.2026 passed by the
High Court of Judicature at Bombay, the High Court granted
permission to the appellant-Rajesh K. Mehta, to travel abroad
for a period of 120 days, subject to certain conditions,

--- Page 113 ---
2
including  a  monetary  condition  of  depositing  a  sum  of
Rs.7,50,00,000/- (Rupees seven crores and fifty lakhs) as an
additional security.
5. Dr. Abhishek Manu Singhvi, learned Senior counsel and Mr.
Devdatt  Kamat,  learned  Senior  counsel  appearing  for  the
appellant – Rajesh K. Mehta submit that the Recovery Officer,
Debts Recovery Tribunal (for short, ‘DRT’) No. II, Mumbai,
himself has modified the earlier order dated 25.10.2023, by
withdrawing the arrest warrant vide order dated 22.07.2025 and
all  other  travel  restrictions  imposed  on  the  appellant.
Therefore, in law, there is no bar. The reason why the
appellant has filed the interim application before the High
Court to travel abroad, was due to the reason that the
respondent - HDFC Bank, by placing reliance upon the previous
order,  had  raised  an  objection  before  the  Immigration
Authorities. The said situation no longer prevails. The mere
fact that the order enuring to the benefit of the appellant
has been challenged and is pending consideration in a writ
petition, cannot be a ground to impose the condition of
depositing  a  sum  of  Rs.7,50,00,000/-  as  an  additional
security. 
6. The appellant has already shown his bonafides in the past by
returning to India, after making frequent visits abroad. His
family resides in Belgium and he has already previously
deposited a sum of Rs.7,50,00,000/- and, in fact, a total sum
of Rs.12 Crores has been deposited or paid so far. All the

--- Page 114 ---
3
properties of the appellant have been secured and the other
conditions imposed by the High Court in the impugned order,
would be sufficient. 
7. In such view of the matter, the condition imposed to deposit
an additional security amount will have to be set aside,
particularly, when there are no criminal proceedings pending
against the appellant – Rajesh K. Mehta. 
8. The learned Senior counsel appearing for the respondent – Bank
would submit that it is a case where the appellant - Rajesh K.
Mehta has not placed the correct facts before this Court.
Therefore, there is no need to entertain the present appeal
seeking grant of the relief sought for. The High Court did
take into consideration the equities, and has passed the
impugned order. It is not factually correct to state that the
properties are available for sale and have been encumbered in
one way or other. Considering the facts governing, especially,
the pendency of the Writ Petition No.3802/2025 challenging the
order(s) passed by the Recovery Officer, DRT-II, Mumbai, there
is  no  need  for  interference  with  the  impugned  order.
Additionally, it is prayed that taking note of the facts, the
very order passed by the High Court will have to be set aside.
9. We have heard the learned counsel appearing for the parties
and perused the records.  
10. It is not in dispute that the appellant did make frequent
travels abroad and returned back to India. He is also not a
flight risk. These two factors, in fact, have been taken note

--- Page 115 ---
4
of by the High Court itself. Additionally, we find that, as on
today, the order of the Recovery Officer, DRT-II, Mumbai dated
22.07.2025 enures to the benefit of the appellant-Rajesh K.
Mehta. 
11. In such view of the matter, there is no bar for the appellant-
Rajesh K. Mehta to travel abroad. However, the High Court has
exercised its discretion by imposing the condition to deposit
an additional sum as security. 
12. In such view of the matter, the only issue for consideration
is whether the said condition imposed by the High Court is
just and proper, since we do not find any merit in the appeal
filed by the Trust, challenging the very permission granted in
favour of the appellant to travel abroad. 
13. It is the submission of the learned Senior counsel appearing
for the appellant-Rajesh K. Mehta that all the properties
belonging to the appellant have been attached and he is not in
a position to comply with the monetary condition imposed vide
the impugned order. While the learned Senior counsel appearing
for the respondent-Bank, by placing reliance upon one of the
orders passed by the High Court, would submit that a factual
finding has been recorded by the Recovery Officer, DRT-II,
Mumbai himself that the appellant has got sufficient financial
means. 
14. Taking note of the aforesaid position, we are only inclined to
modify the condition imposed by the High Court by reducing the
sum of Rs.7,50,00,000/- to a sum of Rs.3,00,00,000/- (Rupees

--- Page 116 ---
5
Three Crores). The appellant-Rajesh K. Mehta is directed to
deposit the modified security amount in the same manner, as
directed by the High Court. The aforesaid compliance will have
to be made within a period of three weeks before undertaking
the proposed travel. 
15. We make it clear that within the time if the appellant comes
back, the same cannot be construed as the complete compliance
of the order, as the ultimate outer limit granted by the High
Court was of 120 days, which enables him to undertake further
travel within the same. 
16. To put an end to the lis in one way or the other, we request
the High Court to make an endeavour to dispose of pending writ
petitions  bearing  W.P.  No.3802/2025  and  W.P.  (L)
No.40817/2025, within a period of six months from the date of
receipt of a copy of this order.  
17. The Presiding Officer, DRT-II, Mumbai is also directed to
dispose of the pending matter being M.A. No.119/2025 in R.P.
No.709/2004, within a period six months from the date of
receipt of a copy of this order.  
18. By way of a clarification, we make it clear that all the
pending proceedings will have to be decided on their own
merits, without being influenced by the observations made in
the impugned order.
19. Both the appeals are disposed of in the aforesaid terms.
20. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.

--- Page 117 ---

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL  NO.         OF 2026
(@ SLP(C) No.25843/2026)
RAJESH K. MEHTA                                    APPELLANT(s)
                                VERSUS
HDFC BANK LIMITED                                  RESPONDENT(S)
WITH
CIVIL APPEAL  NO.         OF 2026
(@SLP(C) No(s).28456/2026)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. Two sets of appeals are placed before us for consideration.
Civil Appeal @ SLP (C) 25843/2026 is filed by the appellant –
Rajesh K. Mehta, aggrieved over the condition imposed by the
High Court, while granting permission to travel abroad and
Civil Appeal @ SLP (C) 28456/2026 has been filed by the
appellant-Lilavati Kirtilal Mehta Medical Trust (for short,
‘the Trust’) after seeking leave, since the said appellant was
not a party before the High Court.
3. These appeals before us lie on a very narrow compass. 
4. By way of the impugned order dated 16.07.2026 passed by the
High Court of Judicature at Bombay, the High Court granted
permission to the appellant-Rajesh K. Mehta, to travel abroad
for a period of 120 days, subject to certain conditions,

--- Page 121 ---
2
including  a  monetary  condition  of  depositing  a  sum  of
Rs.7,50,00,000/- (Rupees seven crores and fifty lakhs) as an
additional security.
5. Dr. Abhishek Manu Singhvi, learned Senior counsel and Mr.
Devdatt  Kamat,  learned  Senior  counsel  appearing  for  the
appellant – Rajesh K. Mehta submit that the Recovery Officer,
Debts Recovery Tribunal (for short, ‘DRT’) No. II, Mumbai,
himself has modified the earlier order dated 25.10.2023, by
withdrawing the arrest warrant vide order dated 22.07.2025 and
all  other  travel  restrictions  imposed  on  the  appellant.
Therefore, in law, there is no bar. The reason why the
appellant has filed the interim application before the High
Court to travel abroad, was due to the reason that the
respondent - HDFC Bank, by placing reliance upon the previous
order,  had  raised  an  objection  before  the  Immigration
Authorities. The said situation no longer prevails. The mere
fact that the order enuring to the benefit of the appellant
has been challenged and is pending consideration in a writ
petition, cannot be a ground to impose the condition of
depositing  a  sum  of  Rs.7,50,00,000/-  as  an  additional
security. 
6. The appellant has already shown his bonafides in the past by
returning to India, after making frequent visits abroad. His
family resides in Belgium and he has already previously
deposited a sum of Rs.7,50,00,000/- and, in fact, a total sum
of Rs.12 Crores has been deposited or paid so far. All the

--- Page 122 ---
3
properties of the appellant have been secured and the other
conditions imposed by the High Court in the impugned order,
would be sufficient. 
7. In such view of the matter, the condition imposed to deposit
an additional security amount will have to be set aside,
particularly, when there are no criminal proceedings pending
against the appellant – Rajesh K. Mehta. 
8. The learned Senior counsel appearing for the respondent – Bank
would submit that it is a case where the appellant - Rajesh K.
Mehta has not placed the correct facts before this Court.
Therefore, there is no need to entertain the present appeal
seeking grant of the relief sought for. The High Court did
take into consideration the equities, and has passed the
impugned order. It is not factually correct to state that the
properties are available for sale and have been encumbered in
one way or other. Considering the facts governing, especially,
the pendency of the Writ Petition No.3802/2025 challenging the
order(s) passed by the Recovery Officer, DRT-II, Mumbai, there
is  no  need  for  interference  with  the  impugned  order.
Additionally, it is prayed that taking note of the facts, the
very order passed by the High Court will have to be set aside.
9. We have heard the learned counsel appearing for the parties
and perused the records.  
10. It is not in dispute that the appellant did make frequent
travels abroad and returned back to India. He is also not a
flight risk. These two factors, in fact, have been taken note

--- Page 123 ---
4
of by the High Court itself. Additionally, we find that, as on
today, the order of the Recovery Officer, DRT-II, Mumbai dated
22.07.2025 enures to the benefit of the appellant-Rajesh K.
Mehta. 
11. In such view of the matter, there is no bar for the appellant-
Rajesh K. Mehta to travel abroad. However, the High Court has
exercised its discretion by imposing the condition to deposit
an additional sum as security. 
12. In such view of the matter, the only issue for consideration
is whether the said condition imposed by the High Court is
just and proper, since we do not find any merit in the appeal
filed by the Trust, challenging the very permission granted in
favour of the appellant to travel abroad. 
13. It is the submission of the learned Senior counsel appearing
for the appellant-Rajesh K. Mehta that all the properties
belonging to the appellant have been attached and he is not in
a position to comply with the monetary condition imposed vide
the impugned order. While the learned Senior counsel appearing
for the respondent-Bank, by placing reliance upon one of the
orders passed by the High Court, would submit that a factual
finding has been recorded by the Recovery Officer, DRT-II,
Mumbai himself that the appellant has got sufficient financial
means. 
14. Taking note of the aforesaid position, we are only inclined to
modify the condition imposed by the High Court by reducing the
sum of Rs.7,50,00,000/- to a sum of Rs.3,00,00,000/- (Rupees

--- Page 124 ---
5
Three Crores). The appellant-Rajesh K. Mehta is directed to
deposit the modified security amount in the same manner, as
directed by the High Court. The aforesaid compliance will have
to be made within a period of three weeks before undertaking
the proposed travel. 
15. We make it clear that within the time if the appellant comes
back, the same cannot be construed as the complete compliance
of the order, as the ultimate outer limit granted by the High
Court was of 120 days, which enables him to undertake further
travel within the same. 
16. To put an end to the lis in one way or the other, we request
the High Court to make an endeavour to dispose of pending writ
petitions  bearing  W.P.  No.3802/2025  and  W.P.  (L)
No.40817/2025, within a period of six months from the date of
receipt of a copy of this order.  
17. The Presiding Officer, DRT-II, Mumbai is also directed to
dispose of the pending matter being M.A. No.119/2025 in R.P.
No.709/2004, within a period six months from the date of
receipt of a copy of this order.  
18. By way of a clarification, we make it clear that all the
pending proceedings will have to be decided on their own
merits, without being influenced by the observations made in
the impugned order.
19. Both the appeals are disposed of in the aforesaid terms.
20. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
(CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION)
 
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.          OF 2026
(Arising out of SLP (Criminal) No. 3845 of 2026)
PRABHA DEVI                                         …Appellant(s)
VERSUS
THE STATE OF BIHAR & ORS.                          …Respondent(s)
O R D E R
Leave granted.
2. The appellant is the mother-in-law of respondent no. 2, the
complainant. The appellant calls in question the final order dated
10.11.2025 passed by the High Court of Judicature at Patna in
Criminal Miscellaneous No.36569 of 2025, to the extent that the
High Court declined to quash the criminal proceedings against her.
The  proceedings  arise  from  FIR  No.  20  of  2024,  dated
27.03.2024, registered at Mahila Police Station, Saran, initially
for offences under Sections 354, 379, 498A and 34 of the Indian
Penal Code, 1860. After investigation, Charge-sheet No. 36 of 2024,
dated 22.07.2024, was filed under Sections 341, 323, 498A, 504 and
34 IPC. Cognizance was taken on 02.09.2024 in T.R. No. 3763 of
2024.
3. The marriage between respondent No.2 and the appellant’s son
was solemnised on 22.11.2015, whereafter the spouses ordinarily
resided at Pune. It is alleged that during the COVID-19 period in
2020, they shifted to the family residence at Bada Telpa Chowk,
Page 1 of 5

--- Page 129 ---
District Saran, where respondent No.2 was subjected to harassment
by the accused persons. 
The material incident concerning the appellant is alleged to
have occurred on 15.02.2023, when respondent no.2 returned with her
father to the matrimonial residence. It is alleged that the
appellant and the sister-in-law abused her and that the appellant
admitted having taken jewellery found missing from an almirah. The
acts of catching respondent no. 2 by her hands and hair, assaulting
her and tearing her clothes are specifically attributed to the
father-in-law and brother-in-law, followed by the general assertion
that all the accused beat her. 
4. The  statements  of  the  complainant's  parents  principally
concern the matrimonial discord between the spouses and do not
attribute to the appellant any specific demand for property or
distinct act causing hurt. Six persons from the neighbourhood
stated that respondent no. 2 ordinarily lived in Pune and that they
had neither seen nor heard of any harassment by the in-laws. The
record discloses no recovery of jewellery and no injury report.
Nevertheless, a common charge sheet was filed against the husband
and four in-laws.
5. In the quashing petition filed by the appellant and the other
in-laws, the High Court held that the allegations against the
father-in-law, brother-in-law, and sister-in-law were general and
omnibus, and it quashed the proceedings against them. However, the
High Court neither quashed the proceedings against the appellant
Page 2 of 5

--- Page 130 ---
nor recorded how the ingredients of the charged offences were made
out against her. 
Instead, the High Court directed the appellant and her son to
participate in mediation, granted interim protection for four
months and made its continuance depend upon which party was
responsible for failure of mediation.
6. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that the allegations
do not disclose the ingredients of the offences appearing in the
charge sheet and that the criminal proceedings could not have been
retained.  Learned  counsel  for  the  respondents  rely  upon  the
allegations of abuse, assault and removal of jewellery. They submit
that the appellant supported her son’s conduct.
7. The Court must examine whether the allegations, taken at their
face  value,  along  with  the  material  collected  during  the
investigation, disclose the ingredients of the offences alleged
against the particular accused. The principles in State of Haryana
v. Bhajan Lal, 1992 Supp (1) SCC 335  and Kahkashan Kausar alias
Sonam v. State of Bihar, (2022) 6 SCC 599 permit interference where
the allegations do not constitute an offence and caution against
compelling relatives of the husband to face trial on general and
omnibus allegations.
Tested on the aforesaid standard, the ingredients of Section
498A IPC are not disclosed against the appellant. No unlawful
demand  is  attributed  to  her.  The  collective  allegations  of
taunting, opposition to the marriage and harassment do not state
Page 3 of 5

--- Page 131 ---
the particular conduct of the appellant or disclose wilful conduct
of the degree contemplated by the provision. The later assertion
that she failed to restrain her son cannot constitute cruelty or
common intention without a corresponding factual foundation in the
FIR or the material collected during investigation.
8. To attract Section 341 IPC, no act of wrongful restraint is
attributed to the appellant. 
As regards Section 323 IPC, the detailed acts of physical
assault are attributed to the father-in-law and brother-in-law,
against whom the criminal proceedings have been quashed by the High
Court in the impunged order. The residual allegation against all
the accused is undifferentiated, does not identify any particular
act of the appellant and is not particularised by the material
collected during investigation. However, the High Court, while
quashing  the  proceedings  against  the  other  in-laws,  did  not
distinguish the case of the appellant or record any reason for
denying the relief of quashing qua the appellant.
For Section 504 IPC, neither the words used nor the facts
showing an intentional insult likely to provoke a breach of peace
are stated. 
Section 34 IPC cannot supply the essential facts of the
principal offences.
9. The allegation concerning the jewellery is undoubtedly more
specific. However, after investigation, no charge under Section 379
IPC or any offence concerning entrustment or dishonest retention of
Page 4 of 5

--- Page 132 ---
the jewellery was filed, and no recovery was effected. In the absence
of the necessary connecting facts, that allegation cannot, by
itself, be transposed into the distinct offences appearing in the
charge-sheet. 
10. We are, therefore, satisfied that the allegations and the
material collected during the investigation do not disclose the
necessary ingredients of Sections 341, 323, 498A and 504, read with
Section  34  IPC,  against  the  appellant.  Continuation  of  the
prosecution against her would amount to an abuse of the process of
law.
11. Consequently, the appeal is allowed. The impugned final order
dated 10.11.2025 is set aside to the extent that it declines
quashing the criminal proceedings as against the appellant herein.
Therefore, all subsequent criminal proceedings/processes arising
out of FIR no. 20 of 2024 dated 27.03.2024 registered at Mahila
Police Station, Saran are quashed only insofar as they concern the
appellant, Prabha Devi.
This  order  shall  not  affect  the  proceedings  against  the
husband, which shall be considered on their own merits.
12. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.      OF 2026
(Arising out of SLP(Crl.) No.2770/2026)
STATE OF HIMACHAL PRADESH REPRESENTED 
BY ITS ADDITIONAL SECRETARY (HOME)
APPELLANT(S)
                              VERSUS
COURT ON ITS OWN MOTION RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The State of Himachal Pradesh is in appeal against the
judgment and order dated 26.04.2024 passed by a Division
Bench of the High Court of Himachal Pradesh, whereby the
application moved by the appellant-State seeking permission
of  the  High  Court  to  withdraw  prosecution  against
sitting/former MPs/MLAs, in terms of the instructions issued
by the State Government in a letter dated 31.12.2022, was
partly allowed, and permission to withdraw prosecution was
granted only in respect of the cases mentioned in the
concluding part of the said judgment, namely, paragraph 58.
3. The occasion for the State to seek prior permission of
the High Court for withdrawal of criminal prosecution arose
in light of the directions contained in paragraph 8 of the
order dated 10.08.2021 passed by this Court in Ashwini Kumar
Upadhyay v. Union of India and Another, ( 2021) 20 SCC 599.
In  the  aforesaid  case,  this  Court,  in  larger  public
1

--- Page 154 ---
interest, directed time-bound conclusion of trial against
sitting or former MPs/MLAs by constituting Special Courts on
a pan-India basis. Such trials were required to be concluded
in a time-bound manner. This Court also issued various
directions concerning the constitution and functioning of
such Special Courts, including that the Presiding Officers
of these Courts shall not be transferred, save and except
upon their superannuation or in exceptional circumstances.
One of the issues considered in the order dated 10.08.2021
was the misuse of the power of the prosecutor to withdraw
cases under Section 321 of the Code of Criminal Procedure,
1973. It was in this context that this Court issued the
following direction: 
“8. In view of the law laid down by this Court, we
deem it appropriate to direct that no prosecution
against  a  sitting  or  former  MP/MLA  shall  be
withdrawn without the leave of the High Court in the
respective suo motu writ petitions registered in
pursuance of our order dated 16.09.2020. The High
Courts are requested to examine the withdrawals,
whether pending or disposed of since 16.09.2020, in
light of guidelines laid down by this Court.”
 
4. It was in deference to the above-stated direction that
the State of Himachal Pradesh approached the High Court
seeking withdrawal of prosecution in 65 cases. Of these,
five cases came to be disposed of while the application was
pending consideration before the High Court, leaving 60
cases for consideration.  Vide  the impugned judgment and
order dated 26.04.2024, the High Court allowed withdrawal of
prosecution in 15 cases and declined the prayer in respect
2

--- Page 155 ---
of the remaining 45 cases. It is, however, a matter of
record that, out of these 45 cases, 4 cases had already
resulted in acquittal/discharge, and 2 had been wrongly
repealed in the application. There were, thus, effectively
39 matters, for which the High Court declined permission to
withdraw prosecution.
5. We find that the cases, where the State applied for
withdrawal of prosecution, can be broadly categorized as
follows:
(i) Cases under Section 269 Indian Penal Code, 1860 (IPC),
registered during COVID-19 pandemic, alleging acts likely to
spread infection of a disease dangerous to life;
(ii)  Cases  under  Section  353  IPC,  alleging  assault  or
criminal force against a public servant during the COVID-19
pandemic, but without there being any instance of injury or
assault having been caused to a public servant;
(iii) Cases under Sections 504 and 506 IPC, alleging breach
of  peace  and  criminal  intimidation  during  the  COVID-19
pandemic;
(iv) Cases under Section 8B of the National Highways Act,
1956, pertaining to dharna, etc., on the National Highway,
during COVID-19 time; and
(v) Cases under Section 51 of the Disaster Management Act,
2005, which also  pertain to incidents  arising during the
COVID-19 pandemic.
6. On perusal of the allegations contained in some of the
FIRs, we find that the incidents in question pertain to the
COVID-19  pandemic  period.  Those  were  exceptional
circumstances, marked by unforeseen conditions, in which
3

--- Page 156 ---
persons, including public representatives, may have reacted
or acted in ways that would not ordinarily have arisen in
normal circumstances. Significantly,  none  of  the  cases
discloses commission of any grave or heinous crime, nor is
there any indication that the accused persons therein are
hardened criminals or have indulged repeatedly in similar
offenses. The allegations against the public representatives
essentially relate to their participation in public dharna
and/or raising the grievances of the general public before
different forums.
7. In our considered view, continuation of prosecutions of
this nature, arising out of special circumstances explained
above, would neither serve the cause of administration of
criminal justice system nor benefit the public interest in
any manner. On the contrary, these proceedings would hamper
the  progress  of  other  serious  and  contentious  matters
pending before the courts, which are required to be decided
timely.
8. We, therefore, see no reason to not accept/allow the
application of the State in entirety for withdrawal of
prosecution in respect of all the cases which remain for
consideration thereunder.
9. For the reasons aforestated, we allow this appeal.
Accordingly, the impugned judgment of the High Court is
modified  to  that  extent  and,  while  allowing  CMP
No.12451/2023, moved by the State of Himachal Pradesh before
4

--- Page 157 ---
the  High  Court,  permission  is  granted  to  withdraw
prosecution in respect of all the cases mentioned in the
said application and remaining for consideration. Ordered
accordingly.

(SURYA KANT)
............................J.
(JOYMALYA BAGCHI)  
............................J.
(V. MOHANA)
      
NEW DELHI;        
SEPTEMBER 09, 2026

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
MISCELLANEOUS APPLICATION NO. 2714 OF 2026
IN
CIVIL APPEAL NO. 7949 OF 2024
THE MANAGING DIRECTOR 
M/S BHARAT RASAYAN 
LIMITED (UNIT-II) APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
ADITYA ROOP SINGH CHAUHAN RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. The present Miscellaneous Application has been registered on
an Office Report dated 10.09.2026 seeking directions regarding the
investment and disbursal of Rs.3,27,82,418/-, presently lying in a
fixed deposit with the Registry of this Court.
2. The National Green Tribunal, Western Zone Bench, Pune (NGT),
by its judgment dated 29.05.2024 in Original Application No.60/2022
(WZ), awarded: (i) additional compensation of Rs.2,75,92,936/- to
the legal heirs of Sudhansusekhara Baman Sadhangi, Kundan Kumar Jha
and Amit Kailasrao Bijawe under paragraphs 108 and 109 read with
paragraph 118(ii); and (ii) additional compensation aggregating to
Rs.17,60,000/- to the injured persons under paragraph 111 read with
paragraph 118(iii).
3. The aforesaid order was challenged before this Court and vide
order dated 02.08.2024, this Court directed the appellant-company
to comply with paragraphs 101 to 112 read with paragraph 118(ii)
and (iii) of the NGT judgment. On 30.08.2024, upon being informed
1

--- Page 160 ---
that the persons entitled to receive compensation were not readily
traceable, this Court directed, as an  ad  hoc  measure, that the
compensation be deposited with its Registry together with interest
at 7 per cent (%) per annum. 
4. The appeal was finally disposed of on 07.08.2026, whereby this
Court declined to interfere with the environmental compensation
imposed by the NGT and directed the Gujarat Pollution Control Board
to spend that amount strictly in accordance with the utilisation
plan disclosed in its affidavit dated 10.07.2026. The final order
did not, however, contain any direction for disbursal of the
accident compensation deposited with the Registry.
5. The Registry has now sought a clarification with respect to
the amount of Rs. 3,27,82,418/-, which is lying deposited with the
same. The said amount(s) have to be paid to the victim-claimants or
their legal heirs, as the case may be. 
6. The  earlier  inability  to  trace  the  beneficiaries  cannot
defeat, or indefinitely postpone, disbursal. We cannot accept the
bald-faced plea taken by the appellant-company that the claimants
are not traceable.  A Court-supervised exercise is necessary to
identify them, verify their entitlement and facilitate payment.
7. Consequently, we request the Chief Justice of the Gujarat High
Court to cause appropriate suo  motu proceedings to be registered
for the following limited purposes:
2

--- Page 161 ---
(i)  identifying  the  injured  persons  referred  to  in
paragraph 111 of the NGT judgment and the legal heirs of
the three deceased employees referred to in paragraphs
108 and 109 thereof;
(ii) verifying their identity and entitlement and, where
necessary, determining the inter se  shares of the legal
heirs, without reopening the quantum of compensation
awarded by the NGT;
(iii) obtaining such records and assistance as may be
required  from  the  appellant-company,  the  relevant
authorities and the District Legal Services Authority,
Bharuch,  and  directing  publication  of  notices  if
considered necessary; and
(iv)  disbursing  the  amounts  due  to  each  verified
beneficiary, together with the proportionate interest
accrued thereon (if any), in accordance with the NGT
judgment and the directions contained in this order.
8. The fixed deposit, which is due to mature on 17.09.2026, shall
be renewed by the Registry for one year from the date of maturity,
together with accrued interest, or until the amount is transferred
pursuant to this order, whichever is earlier.
9. Upon verification, the Registrar General of the High Court
shall forward the beneficiaries' particulars and a requisition to
the Registry of this Court, which shall transfer the amount held in
the  fixed  deposit  to  the  High  Court  for  disbursal.  Any
3

--- Page 162 ---
undistributed balance shall remain in an interest-bearing deposit
under the orders of the High Court.
10. The Registry shall forthwith transmit a copy of this order,
together with the relevant record, to the Registrar General of the
High  Court  of  Gujarat.  The  Miscellaneous  Application  stands
disposed of in the above terms.

(past, present, and future), permanent
alimony, jewelry, other article, movable
and immovable properties etc. and the
petitioner undertakes not to put forth
any further claim towards the same in
future at any stage. 
f. That it is agreed that the parties
shall not interfere in the peaceful life
of each other in any manner whatsoever.
2

They shall not have any communication
with each other by themselves, or through
their  relatives,  after  the  grant  of
divorce,  through  any  means  of
communication  such  as  SMS,  Whatsapp,
Email, post etc.  
6. Therefore, it is clear that the marriage
has irretrievably been broken down with no
possibility of reconciliation. Hence, it is a
fit  case  where  this  Hon’ble  Court  may
exercise its extraordinary powers to grant a
decree of divorce.”
3. The demand draft as mentioned in paragraph 5(e) has
been  handed  over  by  the  respondent’s  counsel  to  the

4. Considering the settlement and the marriage between
the parties having been broken down irretrievably, we are
inclined to allow IA No. 202757/2026 and direct that
marriage between the parties solemnized on 12.12.2013 stand
dissolved by a decree of divorce by mutual consent.

O R D E R
1. During pendency of the present Transfer Petition, the
parties were referred for mediation to be conducted by the
Supreme Court Mediation Centre. Upon a successful
mediation, the parties have entered into a settlement
agreement duly signed by both the parties and the Mediator.
Basing on the settlement agreement, the parties have moved
a joint application i.e. I.A. No. 101189 of 2025 under Article
142 of the Constitution of India for passing a decree of
divorce by mutual consent under Section 13-B of the Hindu
Marriage Act, 1955 and for quashing of the complaint and
petitions filed by the parties against each other.
2. Both the parties are appearing through virtual mode.
They confirm and reiterate the terms of settlement. The
petitioner would state that she has received the total mount
of settlement to the tune of Rs. 18,00,000/- (Rupees
Eighteen Lakhs Only).
3. The parties have set out the terms of settlement which
T.P. (C) No. 1209 of 2024 1

--- Page 201 ---
are reproduced hereunder for ready reference:-
“5. That in view of the comprehensive mediation sessions
held among the parties and their respective advocates, both
the parties have decided not to live together as husband
and wife and have arrived at an amicable settlement on the
following terms and conditions:-
I. That the parties have agreed that the Respondent-
husband shall pay to the Petitioner-wife a total sum of Rs.
18,00,000/- (Rupees Eighteen Lakhs Only) towards child
support and full and final settlement of all her claims
towards her alimony, Stridhan, maintenance (past, present,
future) and any other claim whatsoever. This amount shall
be paid in installments in the name of Master AARAV S NAIR
(Child) through six post dated cheques which have been
handed over by Respondent Husband to the Petitioner Wife
at the time of Execution of the Settlement Agreement. The
details of the said cheques are mentioned in the Settlement
Agreement.
II. It is agreed between the parties that as they are staying
separately since 25.11.2019 i.e. for the last more than five
years and there is an irretrievable breakdown of the
marriage they will move an application jointly before this
Hon’ble Court under article 142 of the Constitution of India
for invoking inherent powers praying for divorce by mutual
consent.
III. It is further agreed between the parties that they will
move an application before this Hon’ble Court for disposal of
all pending cases in various forum mentioned under para 3
of the Settlement Agreement under Article 142 of the
Constitution of India.
That following cases are pending between the parties:-
a) First Appeal (Defective) No. 247 of 2024 before the
Hon’ble High Court of Judicature at Allahabad challenging
order of dismissal dated 03.04.2024 in Matrimonial Case
No. 199 of 2020 filed by the Petitioner Wife before the
Family Court at Kanpur Nagar (U.P.) seeking dissolution of
marriage.
b) Domestic Violence Case bearing No. CMC (DV) No. 315 of
2020 before the Court of the MM-IV, Kanpur Nagar (U.P.) on
07.01.2020.
c) Maintenance Case No. 13 of 2020 Under Section 125 Cr.

Nagar (U.P.).
d) Recovery of Interim Maintenance vide Application No.

--- Page 202 ---
2240 of 2021 filed by the Petitioner Wife on 30.10.2021 U/s
125 (3) Cr. P.C. before Family Court, Kanpur Nagar (U.P.).
e)  Restitution  of  Conjugal  Rights  Case  bearing  No.
MC/7150/2023 filed by the Respondent Husband dated
16.11.2023 at Family Court, Bengaluru (Karnataka)
IV. The Parties have agreed that the child custody shall
remain with the Petitioner wife till their child attains
majority.
V. The parties have agreed that the Respondent husband
will have the option of child visitation rights twice every year
till the child attains majority during the summer/winter
vacation of the child, the details of which shall be shared by
the Petitioner wife to enable him to make arrangements to
meet the child.
VI. That the parties have agreed to close the joint account

accordingly placed the report before this Hon’ble Court.
8. That subject to the aforesaid terms, the parties have
resolved all the disputes amicably in relation to the marriage
and have been left with no claims against each other or their
respective family members.
9. That the parties undertake to abide by the terms and
conditions set out in the Settlement Agreement, which have
been arrived with free will of the parties without any
coercion, duress or collusion and parties undertake not to
raise any dispute whatsoever henceforth.”
4. In view of the settlement between the parties and for
the fact that the marriage between the parties seems to
T.P. (C) No. 1209 of 2024 3

have been irretrievably broken down, we exercise our power
under Article 142 of the Constitution of India to dissolve

in paragraph 5(III) of the interlocutory application shall
stand quashed/closed. Parties shall produce copy of this

this Court, has joined investigation; not only that, he has returned
Rs.13,00,000/- (Rupees thirteen lakh) only to the informant. 
7. Whether  or  not  any  amount  has  been  returned  to  the
complainant need not bear examination here. However, having
regard to the nature of allegations and noting that the appellant has
joined  investigation,  we  are  of  the  opinion  that  custodial
interrogation of the appellant is not necessary and that sufficient
ground exists for the appellant to be admitted to an order for grant
of bail in anticipation of arrest.
8. Accordingly, the impugned judgment and order stands set
aside.
9. It is directed that in the event of the appellant being arrested
in connection with proceedings arising out of the aforesaid FIR, he
shall be released on bail by the arresting/investigating officer/trial
court on terms and conditions to be fixed by the trial court.
10. It is made clear that in the event the appellant breaches any of
the terms and conditions imposed by it, the trial court shall be at
liberty to cancel the bail of the appellant.

--- Page 237 ---
3
11. Needless  to  observe,  the  appellant  shall  not,  directly  or
indirectly, by making inducement, threat or promise, dissuade any
person acquainted with the facts of the case from disclosing such
facts to any police officer or to the court.
12. Also, since the investigation is yet to conclude, we direct that if
the  investigating  officer  calls  upon  the  appellant  to  join  the
investigation, he shall do so by attending the police station failing
which liberty is granted to bring any such omission to the notice of
the trial court and seek cancellation of bail. 
13. We clarify that the observations made in this order and grant of
bail will not be treated as findings on the merits of the case.
14. The appeal is allowed on the above terms.
15.  Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

                                  VERSUS

O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The High Court of Delhi at New Delhi, by the impugned
judgment and order dated 27 th March, 2026, has dismissed the
appellant’s application for bail.
3. Appellant was arrested on 16 th November, 2022 in connection
with FIR No.0092 of 2020 dated 7 th August, 2020 registered at Police
Station Economic Offences Wing (EOW), Delhi under Sections 420,
409, 467, 468, 471 and 120-B of the Indian Penal Code, 1860.
4. We have heard learned counsel appearing for the parties and
perused the materials on record.
5. Chargesheet was filed on 13 th February, 2023. Prosecution
proposed to record the evidence of about 250 witnesses to drive

--- Page 241 ---
2
home the charges against the appellant. Charges have not yet
framed, though three and half years have elapsed since the
chargesheet was filed. Since the trial has not yet commenced, it is
quite likely (having regard to the number of witnesses proposed to be
examined) that the trial is likely to take sufficient time to conclude
after framing of charges. 
6. Since the trial will be a long-drawn process and the appellant
has suffered incarceration for close to four years, further detention in
custody will amount to a punishment without trial. 
7. Taking an overall view of the matter, we are of the considered
opinion that the appellant need not be detained in custody any longer
and that he could be admitted to an order for release on bail pending
trial.
8. Accordingly, we set aside the impugned judgment and order.
9. Appellant shall be released on bail, subject to furnishing of bail
bonds to the satisfaction of the trial court and subject to such other
terms and conditions as may be imposed by it.
10. Needless to observe, the appellant shall not, directly or
indirectly, by making inducement, threat or promise, dissuade any
person acquainted with the facts of the case from disclosing such
facts to the court.
11. In the event there is any breach of the terms and conditions for
grant of bail, the trial court shall be at liberty to cancel the bail of the

--- Page 242 ---
3
appellant.
12. It is also ordered that the appellant shall diligently attend
proceedings of the trial, unless exempted. If he abstains from
attending the proceedings without justifiable cause, that could also be
seen as breach of the conditions for grant of bail and the trial court
will be free to pass appropriate orders.
13. We clarify that the observations made in this order and grant of
bail will not be treated as findings on the merits of the case.
14.  The appeal is, accordingly, allowed on the aforesaid terms.
15.  Pending interlocutory application(s), if any, stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
       CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL No.________ OF 2026
(Arising out of SLP(Criminal) No.7285/2026)
DEEPAK DUBEY                                      Appellant(s)
                             VERSUS
THE STATE OF M.P & ANR.                          Respondent(s)
    O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The appellant has been convicted
for  committing  offence  under  Sections
341, 329 and 427 of the Indian Penal
Code, 1860 and has been awarded maximum
RI for 07 years for offence punishable
under Section 329 of the IPC.
3. Under the impugned order, the High
Court has refused to suspend the sentence
imposed  by  the  Trial  Court  on  the
appellant and release him on bail pending
hearing of the appeal.

--- Page 256 ---
2
4. Referring to the medical report
including the X-ray report of the victim/
complainant, it is argued that only a
hair line fracture in the middle finger
of  the  victim/  complainant  has  been
caused by the appellant and therefore, in
the facts and circumstances of the case,
appellant is entitled to be released on
bail pending hearing of the appeal before
the High Court.
5. Per contra,  learned counsel for
the State would submit that the appellant
has five criminal antecedents therefore,
prayer for suspension of sentence has
rightly been rejected by the High Court.
6. Countering the statement made by
the  learned  counsel  for  the  State,
learned counsel for the appellant would
submit that out of those five criminal
antecedents, appellant has already been
acquitted in four case and in the fifth
one, appellant has already been released
on bail.

--- Page 257 ---
3
7. Considering that the appellant has
already undergone about two years of jail
sentence in the present case and the
appeal before the High Court is of the
year  2024,  therefore,  it  is  least
possible that the appeal will be heard
finally in the near future, we are of the
considered view that it is a fit case to
suspend the sentence imposed upon the
appellant and enlarge him on bail.
8. Accordingly,  the  impugned  order
passed by the High Court is set aside and
it is directed that during the pendency
of the appeal before the High Court, the
sentence imposed upon the appellant shall
remain suspended and he shall be released
on bail in connection with Sessions Trial
No. 37/2019 on such terms and conditions
as may be imposed by the Trial Court.
However, appellant shall co-operate with
the hearing of the appeal before the High
Court.

--- Page 258 ---
4
9. The Appeal stands allowed.
10. Pending applications(s), if any,
shall stand closed.

O R D E R
Heard learned counsel for the parties.
2.  Delay condoned.
3.  At  the  outset,  Mr.  Vikramjit  Banerjee,  learned
Additional Solicitor General submits that he has filed an
affidavit bringing on record the fact that in terms of the
directions of this Court to consider the representation of
the petitioners, if so filed, within six weeks, the said
representations have been disposed of by speaking order(s)
dated 28.08.2026 passed by the Department of Food and
Civil Supplies, Government of Arunachal Pradesh. However,
he fairly submits that the time limit has not been adhered
to  and  for  such  non-adherence,  he  has  tendered
unconditional and unqualified apology.
4. Learned counsel for the petitioners submits that the
consideration is totally erroneous and as copy of the
affidavit has been served to him only on 05.09.2026
(Saturday), he may be permitted some time to file a
rejoinder thereto.
5.  Having  considered  the  matter,  we  find  that  the
direction of this Court being very specific to consider
the representation(s), if so filed by the petitioners and
2

--- Page 262 ---
DIARY NO.19990/2026
dispose of the same within six weeks, has been complied
with and order(s) have been passed, though not within the
time frame fixed, but as apology has been tendered, we are
inclined to accept the same.
6. In such background, more so, when contempt is between
the Contemnor and the Court and any third party, including
the petitioners, only have the liberty to bring it to the
notice of the Court that there has been non-compliance, we
find that a case has been made out for not proceeding with
the Contempt in the present matter.
7. Accordingly, the Contempt Petitions stand disposed of.
8. However, before parting, we record that it shall be
open to the petitioners to challenge the order(s) dated
28.08.2026 that have been passed on their representation
before an appropriate forum in accordance with law.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. This Court passed the following directions in the above said
matter as contained in the signed reportable order:-
“15. …..the Authorized Officer could waive the penalty as
such in extenuating circumstances, necessarily not solely
of financial difficulties and in the event of finding
justification in imposing the penalty, the quantum would be
regulated by the Scheme, as coming out from the Paragraph
32A.
16. We are, hence, in doubt of the proposition laid down in
Horticulture Experiment Station Gonikoppal7 by a Co-ordinate
Bench;  with  due  respect  to  the  learned  Judges.  While
directing the deposit of the dues as computed under the EPF
& MP Act including that levied under Section 7Q of that
Act, we refer the question as to whether there is a
discretion under Section 14B on the Authorized Officer to
levy or not to levy the penalty.
17. We, therefore, direct the Registry of this Court to
place the matter before the Hon’ble the Chief Justice of
India for consideration by a larger Bench. 
18. We make it clear that the reference would not impair
the right of the appellants herein, SRAs, to approach the
Central Board under the Second Proviso of Section 14B. 
4

--- Page 269 ---
Civil Appeal  No.7724/2023
 19. On the request made by the learned Counsel appearing
for the respective appellants, we also deem it fit to
direct the appellants to pay the due amounts under the
EPF & MP Act, along with Section 7Q interest, in four
quarterly instalments, the first instalment starting on
15th December, 2026 and then falling on 15 th March, 2027,
15th June, 2027 and 15 th September, 2027. The interest
accrued under Section 7Q due to the deferred instalments,
would also be levied and communicated by the Authorized
Officer to the SRA after the last instalment is paid,
which would be satisfied before 15th October, 2027. If any
single default is committed, the EPFO can proceed for
recovery.
20. With the above directions, the matter is referred to a
larger Bench.”

respondent-State of Gujarat.

11210062250052/2025 registered with the Cybercrime Police Station,
Surat City, under Sections 391(2), 318(4), 336(2), 338, 336(3),
340(2) 61(2) and 3(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (for
short,  ‘BNS’)  read  with  Sections  66(D)  of  the  Information
Technology Act, 2005.
4. Accusation against the appellant is that he along with the
other accused persons had laundered money to the extent of more
than 800 crores by opening new bank accounts. In this connection,₹
1

--- Page 295 ---
a large number of gullible persons have been duped leading to
number of complaints being filed.

has been in custody.
6. Appellant’s bail application was rejected by the High Court
vide order dated 05.02.2026
7. This Court by order dated 10.08.2026, had issued notice.
8. Learned senior counsel for the appellant submits that all the
remaining accused persons have been granted bail. In fact, they
have been granted bail after rejection of the bail application of
the appellant. He further submits that investigation is complete
whereafter charge sheet has been filed. However, trial has not yet
commenced. Therefore, there is no requirement for keeping the
appellant in custody any further.
9. Per contra learned State counsel submits that though according
to the appellant he had acted under the instructions of one Sheru,
investigation has revealed that there is no such person called
Sheru. In fact, it is the appellant who is the mastermind behind
this large-scale money laundering. However, she fairly submits that
it is a fact that the other accused persons have been granted bail
and charge sheet was filed way back in December 2025. She, however,
submits that if this Court is inclined to grant bail, appellant may
be directed to deposit his passport before the Trial Court since he
was earlier found to be operating from Thailand.
10. Submissions made by learned counsel for the parties have
received the due consideration of the Court.
11. Having regard to the stated facts as noted supra, we are
2

--- Page 296 ---
inclined to grant bail to the appellant.
12. Accordingly, impugned order of the High Court dated 05.02.2026
is set aside and the appellant is directed to be produced before
the jurisdictional Magistrate within a maximum period of 7 days
from today whereafter he shall be released from custody on such
terms and conditions as may be deemed appropriate.
13. Additionally, we direct that appellant should deposit his
passport before the aforesaid learned Magistrate on his release
from custody.
14. Appeal is accordingly allowed.
15. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

1. We have heard Mr. Sanchit Sehgal, learned counsel for
the  appellant  and  Mr.  Davinder  Pal  Singh,  learned

NCT of Delhi.
2. Leave granted.
3. This  appeal  takes  exception  to  the  order  dated
15.05.2026 passed by the High Court of Delhi at New Delhi
(briefly the ‘High Court’ hereinafter), rejecting the
prayer for anticipatory bail of the appellant.
4. It is stated that appellant has been arrayed as an
accused in FIR No.364/2025 registered at Police Station-
Crime Branch, Delhi under Sections 63 and 65 of the
Copyright Act, 1957 read with Sections 349/318(4) of the
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (for short, ‘BNS’).
5. Allegation against the appellant is that he had
1

--- Page 315 ---
indulged in illegal manufacturing, refilling, packaging
and sale of counterfeit Castrol lubricant oil in Delhi.
6. This Court, by order dated 16.06.2026, had issued
notice and directed that no coercive steps shall be taken
against the petitioner.
7. In  the  proceedings  held  on  18.08.2026,  we  had
directed the appellant to appear before the Investigating
Officer on 25.08.2026 at 11:00 AM, further directing
continuance of the interim protection.
8. In  the  hearing  today,  learned  counsel  for  the
appellant submits that pursuant to the order of this Court
dated  18.08.2026,  appellant  had  appeared  before  the
Investigating Officer on 25.08.2026 and had joined the
investigation.
9. While Mr. Singh, learned Addl. Solicitor General does
not dispute this fact, he however reiterates the averments
made by the respondent-State of NCT of Delhi in the
counter affidavit.
10. Be that as it may, since the appellant has joined
investigation,  we  are  of  the  view  that  the  interim
protection granted by this Court vide the order dated
16.06.2026 should be made absolute.
11. That being the position, we set aside the impugned
order dated 15.05.2026 passed by the High Court and make
the  order  dated  16.06.2026  absolute.  However,  the
appellant  shall  continue  to  co-operate  with  the
investigation of the case.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
I.A. Nos.20616-20617 of 2020
1. These applications have been filed by one Arun Kumar Gupta,
Member & Ex-Chairman (Natural Gas Cell), National Chamber of
Industries Association, inter alia, alleging that TTZ Authority and
other official respondents have violated the directions of this
Court as contained in the judgment dated 30.12.1996 by permitting
several existing industrial units in the glass industries sector at
Firozabad to enhance their capacities and new units to be set up. A
consequential order to restrain the authorities from permitting new
industries or enhancement of capacity of existing industries in the
TTZ area has been sought.
2. We find that during pendency of these applications, much water
has flown, especially with the judgment dated 22.04.2025 being
passed by this Court, wherein CEC Report No. 19 of 2025 was
considered and certain directions were issued.
3. In compliance of those directions, the TTZ Authority has filed
an affidavit dated 26.09.2025. We are informed that the Cumulative
Impact Assessment Study Report has also been received on 02.09.2026.
4. Meanwhile, vide another order dated 23.07.2026, passed in IA
No. 22551 of 2025, we have directed the TTZ Authority to process
410 pending applications for establishment/expansion/relocation of
2

--- Page 344 ---
industries, subject to the following safeguards:
(a) In every such meeting, an expert representative of CEC
and an expert representative of NEERI shall be invited, and no
meeting shall take place unless both the subject experts are
present;
(b) In the event one of the two experts objects to the nature
of an industry, namely, classifying it not to be a ‘non-
polluting industry’, such application shall not be accepted
without leave of this Court;
(c) where both the experts (NEERI and CEC) and the TTZ
Authority deliver a unanimous opinion, such applications may
be processed and taken to their logical conclusion strictly in
accordance with law, without any reference to this Court.
5. As may be seen, the TTZ Authority has been directed to
associate expert nominees of the CEC and NEERI in its decision-
making  process.  In  our  considered  opinion,  that  directions
adequately  safeguard  the  apprehension  expressed  in  these
applications filed in the year 2020, which with the passage of time,
have become obsolete. 
6. It goes without saying that the application for a new industry
shall also be examined and processed by the TTZ Authority strictly
in terms of the order dated 23.07.2026, a portion of which has been
quoted above.
7. Any person aggrieved by the decision of the TTZ Authority
shall  be  at  liberty  to  initiate  appropriate  independent
3

--- Page 345 ---
proceedings.  Further,  public-spirited  persons,  like  the
applicant(s), shall also be at liberty to place their viewpoint
before the TTZ Authority, and such suggestions/objections shall
also  be  considered  while  processing  the  applications.  The
expeditious  disposal  of  the  pending  applications  shall  be
appreciated.
8. With liberty aforesaid, these applications are disposed of.

1. Complaint Case No.205/2022 was decided in favour of the petitioner, by
the District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission-VI (New Delhi) 1 by an
order dated 25th November, 2024.
2. The relevant Bench of the DCDRC comprised of Ms. Poonam Chaudhry,
President, and Mr. Bariq Ahmad and Mr. Shekhar Chandra as Members.
3. Respondent before the DCDRC applied for a review. Such petition was
1  DCDRC
1

--- Page 353 ---
allowed on 25 th August 2025 by a Bench of which Ms. Poonam Chaudhry,
President and Mr. Bariq Ahmad, Member constituted the coram.
4. Challenging the order dated 25 th August 2025 allowing the review, the
petitioner approached the High Court with a petition under Article 227 of the
Constitution of India. The impugned order dated 17 th April, 2026 has declined
interference on the ground that Section 41 of the Consumer Protection Act,
2019 permits an appeal against the order dated 25th August, 2025.
5. Before us, learned counsel appearing for the petitioner questions the non-
inclusion of Mr. Shekhar Chandra, Member, who had authored the order dated
25th November, 2024. According to him, Mr. Shekhar Chandra was a Member of
the DCDRC on 25th August, 2025; and, this is revealed from an order authored
by him on 30th October 2025 while disposing of Case No.CC 505/2016.
6. Regulation 15 of the Consumer Protection (Consumer Commission
Procedure) Regulations, 2020 provides as follows:-
“15.Review.-(1) It shall set out clearly the grounds for review.
(2) Unless otherwise ordered by the Consumer Commission, an
application for review shall be disposed of by circulation without
oral arguments, as far as practicable between the same
members who had delivered the order sought to be reviewed.”
7. Without entering into the merits of the controversy raised by the
petitioner in the special leave petition, we are desirous of ascertaining from the
DCDRC the reason as to why Mr. Shekhar Chandra, Member, who had authored
the order dated 25 th November 2025, was not included in the Bench which
decided the review petition of the respondent.
8. Let a report in this regard be called for from the Registry of the DCDRC for
our consideration.

Petition(s) for Special Leave to Appeal (Crl.)  No(s).  8111/2026
[Arising out of impugned final judgment and order dated  18-11-2025
in CRM-M No. 43706/2022 passed by the High Court of Punjab &

CENTRAL BUREAU OF INVESTIGATION                    Petitioner(s)
                                VERSUS
STATE OF PUNJAB & ORS.                             Respondent(s)
 
Date : 31-08-2026 This petition was called on for hearing today.
CORAM : 
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE M.M. SUNDRESH
         HON'BLE  MR. JUSTICE PRASANNA B. VARALE
For Petitioner(s) Mr. Anil Kaushik, A.S.G.
                   Mr. Shreekant Neelappa Terdal, AOR
                   Mr. Pranjal Singh, Adv.
                   Mr. Aman Jha, Adv.
                   Mr. Raman Yadav, Adv.
                   Ms. Priyanka Tyagi, Adv.

For Respondent(s) Mr. Vivek Jain, A.A.G.
                  Ms. Nupur Kumar, AOR
                  Mr. Sadiq Noor, Adv.
                   
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
We have heard the learned ASG appearing for the
petitioner-CBI and the learned AAG appearing for the
respondent-State of Punjab. 
We  have  also  perused  the  impugned  judgment
passed by the High Court.
Learned ASG submits that the High Court has
proceeded on an erroneous premise. What has been
sought for is the forwarding of the trial records

--- Page 362 ---
2
that were otherwise pending on the file of the
Special  Court,  Amritsar  in  Case  No.NDPS/29/2018,
proceedings of which have been closed vide the order
dated 21.01.2023, to the proceedings pending before
the  designated  CBI  Court  at  Mohali  wherein  the
proceedings qua the two FIRs are pending.
Learned AAG appearing for the respondent-State
would submit that it is not correct to state that
the proceedings in case No.NDPS/29/2018 is closed.
Having heard the parties, we have specifically
taken note of the order passed by the Judge of the
Special  Court,  Amritsar  in  Case  No.NDPS/29/2018,
dated 21.01.2023, with specific regards to paragraph
4 which reads as under:
“4. Thus, without commenting anything on
the actual facts and circumstances of the
case  and  taken  into  consideration  the
directions issued by the Hon’ble High Court
in  CRM  M  No.3144-2018(O&M)  decided  on
12.01.2021 and further in light of the status
submitted by Inspector Balwinder Singh CBI
Chandigarh  that  the  final  report  under
Section 173 of Cr.P.C. has been filed before
the Ld. CBI, Court, Mohali. So, this Court is
of the opinion that nothing has been left in
the present case, as accused persons are
already facing the trial before the Ld. CBI
Court. So, taken into consideration that the
FIR has been transferred by the Hon’ble High
Court,  present  case  is  ordered  to  be
consigned to record room, being not required

--- Page 363 ---
3
for further proceedings, by this Court, as
accused persons cannot face trail in two
courts simultaneously, on the basis of the
same facts of the case. Accused persons are
directed to appear before the ld. CBI Court.
File be consigned to record room.”
In view of the above order, we hold that the
aforesaid proceedings have been closed. What is left
are the two proceedings before the designated CBI
Court at Mohali.
In such view of the matter, there will be no
difficulty in transferring the records which has
been consigned on the file of the Special Court,
Amritsar in Case No.NDPS/29/2018, in pursuant to the
order  of  the  Special  Court,  Amritsar  dated
21.01.2023.
Accordingly, the aforesaid records which had
been consigned in the aforesaid proceedings in Case
No.NDPS/29/2018 stand transferred to the designated
Court at Court of Special Judge, CBI-01, SAS Nagar,
